pool.prompt: On a RUS-financed project, if the buyer does not specify MFD, what must all single-mode fiber be manufactured to at 1310 nm?
pool.explanation: 7 CFR 1755.902 specifies 9.2 um +/- 0.5 um at 1310 nm as the default unless the buyer specifies otherwise, keeping all reels within an 8.7-9.7 um window and limiting splice mismatch loss across a multi-reel project.

pool.prompt: ICEA S-87-640 defines a standard installation tensile rating for OSP fiber cable. What is the commonly cited value?
choices: 2,670 N (approximately 600 lbf)
1,000 N (approximately 225 lbf)
5,340 N (approximately 1,200 lbf)
890 N (approximately 200 lbf)
pool.explanation: ICEA S-87-640 defines 2,670 N (~600 lbf) as the standard installation tensile rating for OSP fiber cable, with a lighter-construction tier commonly cited around 1,330 N (~300 lbf). Exceeding the rated tensile during a pull risks fiber damage. Verify against the current edition before design lock.
pool.citation: ICEA S-87-640 — exact figure sourced from secondary/vendor technical literature this session, not independently confirmed against the paywalled primary standard text; treat as UNVERIFIED-EXACT and verify against the current edition.

pool.prompt: What is the key difference between qualification testing and acceptance testing under RUS/ICEA cable standards?
choices: Qualification is done in the field; acceptance is done in the factory
Qualification is done once per cable design (before production begins); acceptance is done on each production lot to verify ongoing conformance
Qualification tests optical performance; acceptance tests mechanical performance only
Qualification is required by ICEA; acceptance is required only by RUS
pool.explanation: Qualification testing proves the design itself meets the standard, done once per new design. Acceptance testing verifies each production lot (or a statistical sample) continues to conform. Both are required on RUS projects.

pool.prompt: Match each cable parameter to its correct requirement from 7 CFR 1755.902.

targets.label: Fiber color coding (so each fiber is distinguishable)

pool.explanation: 7 CFR 1755.902 covers all three: MFD default (9.2 +/- 0.5 um at 1310 nm, independently confirmed this session), the standard fiber coating OD (250 um is a near-universal industry base value), and the requirement that fiber color coding make every fiber individually identifiable — consistent with the TIA-598 12-color scheme referenced elsewhere in this course.

pool.prompt: A cable coating diameter reads 242 um on a production test report, against a 7 CFR 1755.902-style tolerance of 250 +/- 15 um. Does this conform, and what is the lower limit of the acceptable range?
choices: Conforms; lower limit = 240 um
Conforms; lower limit = 235 um (250 - 15)
Does not conform; 242 um is below the lower limit
Cannot be determined without knowing the fiber's core diameter
pool.explanation: 250 - 15 = 235 um (lower limit); 250 + 15 = 265 um (upper limit). A measurement of 242 um falls within the 235-265 um range, so it conforms.

pool.prompt: Why does RUS specify a default MFD tolerance (9.2 +/- 0.5 um) even when a specific buyer hasn't stated their own requirement?
choices: To make the specification legally void if unspecified

To ensure a baseline consistency across all fiber reels manufactured for RUS-funded projects, limiting splice-mismatch loss when reels from different production runs are joined — the default protects project quality even absent a buyer-specific spec
Because MFD has no actual effect on splice quality
Because RUS requires every project to use exactly the same fiber manufacturer
pool.explanation: Without a default, fiber from different manufacturers or production runs could have MFD values scattered widely, causing unpredictable splice-loss spikes when reels are joined mid-project. RUS's default tolerance provides a floor of consistency across all RUS-funded fiber, protecting project quality even when the buyer hasn't specified their own tighter requirement.

pool.prompt: Why are BOTH qualification testing and acceptance testing required on a RUS project, rather than just one or the other?
choices: They test the same thing and having both is pure redundancy with no added value

Qualification proves the cable DESIGN itself meets the standard (a one-time check before any production begins), while acceptance testing catches manufacturing-process drift or lot-specific defects that could occur even with a qualified design — the two checks cover different failure modes
Qualification is only required for armored cable; acceptance is only required for dielectric cable
Only qualification testing is actually required; acceptance testing is optional under RUS rules
pool.explanation: Qualification testing validates that a cable design, as engineered, meets the standard — but it doesn't guarantee every subsequent production lot will be manufactured correctly. Acceptance testing on each lot (or a statistical sample) catches manufacturing-process issues that qualification testing, being a one-time design check, cannot detect.

pool.prompt: A production lot's cable tensile rating tests at 2,200 N, below the ~2,670 N (600 lbf) standard installation rating cited for ICEA S-87-640. What should happen to this lot?
choices: Ship it anyway — tensile rating is a suggestion, not a requirement

The lot fails acceptance testing for that parameter and should not be used for standard-tension pulls without further evaluation — exceeding a cable's actual rated tensile during installation risks fiber damage
The rating discrepancy is irrelevant since qualification testing already passed
Automatically re-classify the cable as a lighter-duty tier without any further testing
pool.explanation: Acceptance testing exists precisely to catch a production lot that doesn't meet its rated specification, even if the design was previously qualified. A lot testing below its rated tensile strength should not be treated as meeting spec — using it for a standard-tension pull risks exceeding its actual (lower) capacity and damaging the fiber during installation.
